1109-love-s-labour-s-lost:
Four young lords of Navarre swear off women, wine, and sleep for three years of study, and four ladies of France arrive the same day to wreck the oath. William Shakespeare's early comedy turns on wit duels, love letters gone astray, and a pedant schoolmaster's pageant. The verse sparkles with puns and wordplay.

The lords woo in disguise, the ladies see through them, and the play ends not with weddings but with a death and a year's delay. That sober close sets it apart from other comedies. The play delights lovers of language, and it shows Shakespeare already master of comic form.
1135-the-tempest:
Prospero, the deposed Duke of Milan, lives exiled on an island with his daughter Miranda, ruling spirits and the wild Caliban by magic. When his enemies sail past, he raises a storm, wrecks them ashore, and stages his revenge, only to choose pardon in the end. William Shakespeare's last solo play is his most musical.

Ariel's songs, Caliban's curses, and Miranda's wonder at "brave new world" give the play its glow. Prospero breaks his staff and frees his servant, closing Shakespeare's career with a farewell to art itself. The play still enchants stage, film, and classroom alike.
125-a-girl-of-the-limberlost:
Elnora Comstock collects moths in the Limberlost swamp to pay for her schooling. Gene Stratton-Porter's Girl of the Limberlost follows Elnora as she defies her bitter mother and earns her way. Philip Ammon helps her hunt, and Wesley and Margaret Sinton mother her.

Edith Carr, a city rival, tests Elnora's heart, while Freckles, now grown as Terence O'More, returns. Moth lore, swamp beauty, and the Golden Rule shape the story. Elnora's patience wins love and learning alike. The novel pairs with Freckles as a Limberlost classic. Nature writing and moral earnestness made Stratton-Porter's novels popular with young readers.
1296-the-provost:
John Galt tells the chronicle of a Scottish burgh through its provost, Pawkie, a canny, self-serving magistrate who guides his town through fifty years of change. The tale moves from elections to riots, from new streets to old customs, all in Pawkie's own sly voice.

Galt writes Scots town life with humor and realism, and the provost's memoirs form a social history in miniature. The book, a companion to The Annals of the Parish, shows Galt's gift for local life. It suits readers who like Scottish chronicles and sly narrators.
1320-criminal-psychology-a-manual-for-ju:
Hans Gross was an Austrian jurist who founded modern criminal investigation. He writes this manual for judges and lawyers on how minds work in court: how witnesses err, how suspects lie, and how judges deceive themselves. The book draws on cases and on the new science of mind.

Gross argues that law must learn from psychology if justice is to be just, and his chapters on memory, emotion, and proof still read with force. The manual shaped police work and legal study. It draws readers who like law, mind, and the roots of forensic science.
1409-the-soul-of-the-far-east:
Percival Lowell's study contrasts Western and Eastern ways of mind, drawing on life in the Far East. Eight chapters take up, in turn, individuality, family, adoption, language, nature and art, religion, and imagination. They argue that Eastern life rests far more on the group and on custom than on the single self.

Lowell writes as a clear-eyed outsider, noting manners, speech, and art with care, and he often turns the mirror back on Western habits too. The book is dated in some of its claims, yet it remains a readable early attempt to explain a whole culture through its daily forms and thoughts.
1453-the-alkahest:
Balzac's novel, also called The Quest of the Absolute, follows Balthazar Claes, a Flemish chemist. He ruins his family in search of the alkahest, a universal solvent that would turn base matter to gold. His wife watches their fortune melt in furnaces and experiments, while his children grow up in the shadow of his dream.

The book studies obsession with scientific patience: years of failure, brief hope, and a final discovery that comes too late to save the house. Balzac treats Claes with pity as well as awe. It is a powerful tale of genius, waste, and the price of a single consuming idea.
1510-love-s-labour-s-lost:
In Navarre, a king and three lords swear off love, food, and sleep for three years of study, and then a French princess and her ladies arrive on state business. Vows crumble at once, and the play becomes a sparkling contest of sonnets, puns, and disguises between would-be scholars and witty women.

A pageant of the Nine Worthies ends in farce, and news of a death turns comedy sober at the close, with marriages deferred for a year of trial. The play is Shakespeare's most verbal comedy, full of wordplay and high spirits. It rewards readers who enjoy language as a game.
1540-the-tempest:
Shakespeare's late romance opens with a storm at sea, raised by Prospero, the exiled Duke of Milan, who rules a lonely island with his daughter Miranda and his spirits Ariel and Caliban. A ship carrying his usurping brother Antonio wrecks on the shore, and Prospero's magic sets a reckoning in motion.

Through love between Miranda and Ferdinand, Caliban's rebellion, and Ariel's songs, Prospero moves from vengeance to forgiveness and gives up his art. The play is brief, musical, and full of wonder. It is often read as Shakespeare's farewell to the stage, and a meditation on power and mercy.
1550-a-lady-of-quality-being-a-most-curi:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's historical romance, told as a history related by Mr Isaac Bickerstaff, follows Clorinda Wildairs, a lady of quality in the reign of William and Mary. From a wild girlhood in November 1690, Clorinda grows into a beauty of wit, temper, and daring, courted and quarrelled over by great men.

Through duels, marriages, and the fashions of the town, the novel traces a woman who refuses to be tamed by convention, yet longs for a love equal to her spirit. Burnett writes with colour and sympathy. The book is a lively costume romance, and a portrait of a heroine ahead of her age.
1574-historic-girls-stories-of-girls-who:
E. S. Brooks's Historic Girls tells stories of girls who influenced the history of their times, written in an age of debate over women's equality and rights. The preface argues that women and girls, even in the distant past, proved themselves by action and endeavour, and each chapter follows one such girl through a crisis of her age.

The tales range across countries and centuries, with history retold as adventure for young readers. Brooks writes with earnest admiration. The book is a period work of girls' history, charming in its purpose and a window on how 1880s America taught heroism to girls.
1654-an-unsocial-socialist:
Sidney Trefusis is a rich young man who preaches socialism while living off the very wealth he denounces. This early Shaw novel tests him against the people around him. At an English country house he meets Agatha Wylie, a clever schoolteacher, and the pair trade arguments about class, marriage, and honest work.

Shaw uses the romance to stage debates: can a man be sincere while keeping his money. Can love survive when both partners insist on seeing through each other. The novel is talkative by design, and its comedy comes from Trefusis himself, a reformer whose sharpest opponent is his own comfort.
1665-derrick-vaughan-novelist:
Edna Lyall tells this story through a friend of the title character, a young novelist whose talent grows out of sympathy rather than ambition. Derrick Vaughan spends his early years caring for a drunken father, and the patience that costs him shapes the way he writes about other people's lives.

The narrator, by contrast, admits his own selfishness, and the contrast between the two men drives the book. Lyall's point, borrowed from Lewes and Toynbee, is that a great artist needs deep feeling for others. The novel tests that claim in ordinary scenes: a sickroom, a country house, and a friendship that forces its teller to judge himself.
1725-heart-of-the-west:
Texas ranches, border towns, and the camps of cowboys and rangers replace O. Henry's New York streets in these stories, though the last-page turn stays the same. A ransom is negotiated, a handbook of courtship is put to comic use, a princess meets a puma, and a call loan comes due at the worst hour.

The tales keep O. Henry's signature move — the last-page turn that reorders the whole story. But the ground is new: wide country, dry humor, and men who talk big and act bigger. Readers who know his New York stories will enjoy seeing the same wit at work under a western sky, with sentiment kept just short of soft.
1735-sophist:
How can anyone say what is false, if saying it means saying what is not. The Stranger from Elea takes that riddle as his starting point. The Eleatic Stranger leads the talk, with almost no description of time or place. The argument turns on verbs and nouns: no sentence can be formed without both, as in 'Theaetetus sits. '.

From that small point the dialogue builds a theory of being and not-being, and a way to separate the sophist from the philosopher. It is hard reading, but it is the dialogue where Plato's logic grows teeth. Readers who want the metaphysics behind the Republic's arguments about truth will find the groundwork laid here.
1803-wyoming-a-story-of-the-outdoor-west:
A rifle cracks from a clump of bushes a hundred yards away. The bullet cuts a line between Bannister on one side and Miss Messiter and her foreman on the other. The Lazy D ranch, a dance at Fraser's, and a party call carry the story into the range wars and cattle business of Wyoming.

Raine writes the outdoor west with the confidence of a man who knew its codes: loyalty to a ranch, quick shooting, and women who hold their own in a hard country. The novel moves fast, and its set pieces — ambushes, rides, and confrontations on open ground — give it the shape of the classic ranch romance.
19877-jack-haydon-s-quest:
Jack Haydon's Quest is a school story of Rushmere School. Jack is prefect there and captain of the first fifteen. He walks swiftly out of the school gates one day. His leave takes him to Longhampton, three miles away. A day-scholar friend lies on the sick list there. The errand of friendship launches his quest in earnest.

School stories made prefects into knights of a small realm. Rugby, honor, and loyalty were their working virtues. A quest beyond the gates tests all three. John Finnemore wrote many such tales for boys. His schools run on fairness enforced by heroes. This opening is the genre in miniature. Readers of Tom Brown will know the country.
19967-beauty-and-the-beast:
Beauty and the Beast is the classic fairy tale, retold here anonymously. The merchant's family has fallen into poverty. With no servants, the girls must work hard, like peasants. The sons cultivate the fields to earn their living. All live roughly clothed and simply. That fall from wealth sets Beauty's story in motion. A stolen rose will carry her to the Beast's castle.

Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont's version shaped this tale for children. Her Beauty is virtuous, dutiful, and brave in that order. The Beast's courtesy slowly disproves his appearance. Generations learned the tale in forms close to this one. Its lesson, that worth hides under roughness, never dates. This retelling keeps the familiar bones clean.
20018-evenings-at-donaldson-manor-or-the:
Maria J. McIntosh wrote Evenings at Donaldson Manor, also called The Christmas Guest. Its frame gathers guests for Christmas evenings of talk and tales. A quoted review praises McIntosh's Woman in America warmly here. She has written a clever book, the Protestant Churchman says. It contains much good word and truth, the review continues. American ladies are urged to consider her thoughts carefully. The manor evenings continue that improving vein.

McIntosh was a popular Southern writer of moral fiction. Her Christmas frame lets stories teach without sermonizing directly. Donaldson Manor's guests debate conduct, faith, and feeling nightly. The format suits holiday reading by the fire. American ladies were her declared audience and market. The book shows domestic fiction's respectable power.
20022-sequil-or-things-whitch-aint-finis:
Henry A. Shute wrote Sequil in 1904 as the sequel to his Plupy books. Its narrator Plupy keeps a diary in cheerfully bad spelling. He has forgot whether it was brite and fair since his last diry, he writes. Anyway, it is brite and fair today; lots of things have happened. Beany's father is a policeman now, which makes Beany feel pretty big. Plupy warns Beany had better not say much to him anyway.

Shute, a New Hampshire judge, wrote the Real Diary of a Real Boy first. Its misspelled boyhood became a national delight. Sequil continues Plupy's schoolboy wars, pranks, and loyalties. The comedy lives in the spelling and the deadpan alike. Grown readers remembered their own diaries in his. These books are American boyhood classics of their decade.
20198-lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the:
George Borrow wrote Lavengro, subtitled The Scholar, The Gypsy, The Priest. Lavengro tells, in part, of Borrow's own wild and bookish youth. He learned Romani, roamed with Gypsies, and sold Bibles in Spain. Critics praise how such writers pour their whole selves into their books.

Lavengro blends memoir, tale, and talk on language, roads, and faith. Its hero drifts between scholars, priests, tinkers, and horse dealers. Few English books mix such worlds with so odd a charm. Readers get a classic ramble through words, roads, and Romani life. Borrow's own life, wild and learned, remains the book's true and lasting center throughout.
2033-the-unknown-guest:
Maurice Maeterlinck, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos, writes on the unknown guest, the unseen presence that visits minds in dreams, premonitions, and strange coincidences. Maeterlinck, a Nobel laureate, treats the occult with philosophy. Maeterlinck won the Nobel Prize in 1911, for plays and essays on the unseen.

He asks whether such guests are spirits, thoughts, or powers of the mind itself, weighing evidence with calm curiosity. The book suits readers of mysticism who want speculation grounded in reflection, not mere marvels. His unknown guest, visiting in dreams and omens, asks whether mind reaches beyond body.
2055-two-years-before-the-mast:
Richard Henry Dana Jr., a Harvard student who shipped before the mast for his health, gives a firsthand account of life aboard merchant sailing ships in the 1830s. He sailed round Cape Horn to California, then a remote Mexican province. Dana left Harvard for the voyage in 1834, hoping sea air would mend his eyesight.

Dana describes hard work aloft, floggings, bad food, and the trade in hides, in plain language that sailors praised for its truth. The book helped reform seamen's conditions, and it remains the classic American memoir of common life at sea. His plain account of flogging and hard food helped reformers press for better laws for sailors.
20860-the-butterfly-s-ball-and-the-grass:
Praise from the Pall Mall Gazette fronts The Butterfly's Ball and the Grasshopper's Feast. Children, it notes, may spurn fine new picture books for plain old Goody Two-Shoes. That charm of the old and homely sets this slight book's tone.

William Roscoe's verse ball of insects dates to the early 1800s. Butterflies dance, grasshoppers feast, and small beasts hold a gay ball. The poem ranks among the first true picture-book verses for children. Its light lines and beast pageantry paved the way for the animal picture books children still love today.
21033-sketch-of-the-mythology-of-the-nor:
Desert sands, furnace blasts, floods, and fire rivers scour the lands in this mythology sketch. John Wesley Powell opens his study of North American Indian myth with nature's vast force. Fruits shrivel before starved men's eyes as rivers rage and mountains burst.

Powell, who ran the Colorado River, led the Bureau of Ethnology's early work. This first annual report sketch sorts native myths by the powers they name. Sun, storm, beast, and hero tales take ordered place in his scheme. Scholars have revised his frame since, yet the sketch stays a landmark of the field's bold, early reach.
21133-true-to-his-colours-the-life-that-:
Crossbourne, a quiet village among hills, is the scene of the Reverend Theodore P. Wilson's tale of a sceptic's home. Wilson sets his story some forty years before he wrote, in a place that seemed to hide from the roaring traffic around it. A stream runs restlessly through the village day and night.

True to His Colours argues, in story form, for the life that wears best: steady Christian faith over drink and doubt. Long sermons run through the narrative, as Wilson's readers expected from his temperance fiction. The village cast works out questions of belief, drink, and duty in their daily rounds and troubles.
21298-the-black-tor-a-tale-of-the-reign-:
Two teenage boys from feuding families meet among the wild hills of Derbyshire's Peak District. George Manville Fenn sets their tale in the reign of James the First, their families locked in a centuries-old feud. Each lives in a castle above the moors. A band of ex-soldiers camps on the hills and descends to rob the poorer folk.

The boys form a secret alliance, gathering their fathers' workmen into a small private army against the raiders. Their first attack fails badly. With better weapons and a better plan they try again. Fenn sets honour, inherited hate, and common danger against each other, letting the feud's youngest heirs end what their fathers could not.
21311-gil-the-gunner-the-youngest-office:
Gilbert Vincent goes out to India as a very young soldier in George Manville Fenn's long tale of the East. Schoolboy fights open the book before the regiment sails. In India, battles follow in quick order, and Gil is wounded, knocked out, and recovering as often as he fights.

At one point a wealthy local rajah captures Gil and treats him like an honoured guest, offering him any jewels he likes. Gil refuses, saying freedom to return to his father in the regiment is worth more than gems. The fighting aims at pushing the British out of India, and Fenn follows its cost on both sides.
21313-in-honour-s-cause-a-tale-of-the-da:
Frank Gowan, seventeen, is a page in the Prince of Wales's anteroom at the court of George the First. His father serves in the King's Guard, while fellow page Andrew leans Jacobite, like his father. George Manville Fenn fills the Hanoverian court with German and Dutch courtiers the king brought for comfort.

A German baron deliberately insults Frank's father, and their duel leaves the baron badly wounded. Though loyal to the king, Sir Robert Gowan is sentenced to lose his regiment and leave the country. Frank's search for his father runs through rooftop escapes, spies, and disguises around St James's Palace and its park.
21378-yussuf-the-guide-or-the-mountain-b:
Lawrence, a consumptive boy in his late teens with no relations, wishes aloud for a holiday somewhere hot and sunny. His doctor and a retired professor agree to take him to Asia Minor to see the antiquities, under his lawyer guardian's eye. George Manville Fenn sends the party first to Greece.

Dishonest ship crews sour the start, though their luggage went safely ahead. In Turkey they hire Yussuf, a charming and resourceful guide, and travel inland as helpfulness thins town by town. Mountain bandits capture the party at last and demand a ransom. Yussuf's skill becomes their best hope, in Fenn's tale of sickness, travel, and escape.
21384-afar-in-the-forest:
A young settler tells the tale in W. H. G. Kingston's Afar in the Forest, a short novel of life in the wild woods. He hunts game for the family store while his Uncle Mark fells tall trees around their home. Bit by bit, the two clear land at their new place.

Much of the book is Uncle Mark's own story, told by the fire at night. He tells why the family left home, how they landed safe, and how they found an old settlement in ruins. Lost kin, hidden ties, and two rescued children give the tale its twists. Kingston keeps the cast tangled on purpose, so close reading pays off.
2145-ben-hur-a-tale-of-the-christ:
Lew Wallace tells of Judah Ben-Hur, a Jewish prince of Jerusalem wronged by his Roman friend Messala, sent to the galleys, and raised again through a sea fight and a chariot race. The tale runs beside the life of Christ. Wallace, a Civil War general, wrote Ben-Hur in the 1870s, and it sold for decades.

Wallace opens with wise men in the desert, follows Ben-Hur through Rome and Israel, and closes with faith and forgiveness. Ben-Hur became one of the best-selling novels of the nineteenth century, and a lasting popular epic. The chariot race, Ben-Hur's revenge on Messala, became one of fiction's most famous scenes.
21464-the-gilpins-and-their-fortunes-a-s:
Two school leavers talk over their futures at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Gilpins. One Gilpin boy dreams, with his brother, of farming in Australia like their hard-working father. The brothers sail, and their luck turns on a Sydney quay.

There they save a family from a carriage with bolting horses, and win strong friends. The friends place them as overseers of a run-down sheep and cattle station past the Blue Mountains. The old manager was a crook, and many hands, sent out for crimes, are idle or worse. Mutiny brews before the brothers can set things right.
21493-twice-lost:
Godfrey Rayner's father, a half-pay naval lieutenant, joins a Bristol merchant house in W. H. G. Kingston's Twice Lost. The boy ships as a midshipman on the Heroine for the Pacific. There the tale's lost boy, Harry, first comes into view.

Islanders hold a shipwrecked sailor, and Harry proves to be an English boy used as a pearl diver. The crew takes him aboard and frees him from cruel masters. Years later the party settles in Australia, on the station next to Harry's own parents. Chance and grit drive this warm, tidy tale of loss and return.
21495-to-the-west:
Two young clerks quit a tyrant of an auctioneer in George Manville Fenn's To the West. They set their sights on British Columbia, far across the sea. The way there runs round Cape Horn to San Francisco, then up the coast.

On the road they meet folk good and bad, as Fenn's heroes always do. At last they reach the north and turn to hunting gold. Fenn draws places he never saw with striking life and care. The book runs long for him, some fifteen hours read aloud, and keeps its pace through storms, claims, and close calls.
21558-the-children-of-the-new-forest:
King Charles flees toward the New Forest as Captain Marryat's The Children of the New Forest opens. Marryat published the tale in 1847, his twenty-fourth book and the last of his lifetime. It was written for children and has stayed in print ever since.

When their father falls for the king, the Beverley children hide in a forester's cottage. They learn to farm, hunt, and live by their own hands. Roundhead foes and loyal friends test their courage and wit. The book's blend of history, woodcraft, and family love made it a lasting classic of children's fiction.
21676-confessions-of-a-caricaturist:
Oliver Herford confesses his art in Confessions of a Caricaturist, published in 1917 and dedicated to William Dean Howells. Short verses sit beside drawings of famed men, from Napoleon to Saint Paul. Herford likes Napoleon best, he says, since one hand hides in his vest.

Drawing hands, he owns, is not his knack, and Napoleon spares him the trouble. Roosevelt, Kipling, Shaw, Morgan, and Rockefeller take their turns in rhyme. Even Dante gets a joke about Benedictine and Chianti. Herford's light touch made him the wittiest pen-and-pencil man of his New York circle.
21734-the-golden-dream-adventures-in-the:
Gold in the far West draws the cast of this Ballantyne adventure across an ocean and a continent. The golden dream of the title is the hope of quick wealth that pulled thousands west in his century. Ballantyne knew the wild side of North America from his own years in Canada. He sets green newcomers against a land that tests every promise it seems to make.

The tale follows the party through travel, work, and danger in the western wilds. Greed, luck, and friendship pull the story in turn. Ballantyne keeps his moral steady: wealth found too fast can cost more than it pays. Young readers of his day took the warning with the adventure, gladly.
21753-the-norsemen-in-the-west:
Greenland eight or nine hundred years ago opens this Ballantyne tale of the Norsemen who reached America before Columbus. Two shaggy figures in bear-like dress creep over a ridge above a small hamlet of cottages, sheds, sheep, and boats. A sturdy settler plays with his small son outside the main cottage. The scene sets a whole lost world in motion.

Ballantyne follows the Norse settlers west from Greenland toward the new lands beyond the sea. Voyages, meetings with native peoples, and the hardships of a far colony fill the tale. He wrote it to give boys a true old story: that Europeans crossed the Atlantic long before Columbus. History and adventure sail in the same boat here.
21823-the-butterfly-s-ball-and-the-grass:
Tiny field creatures gather for a feast in this small book of verse by R. M. Ballantyne, published in 1874 for very young children. The gadfly blows his trumpet to call the company: beetle, emmet, gnat, and dragonfly all come in their colors. Predators lay aside their wars for the day and join the dance. A few over-eager dancers cause small mishaps, all safely mended.

Ballantyne wrote half a dozen such books for the youngest readers, some under the name Comus. This one is perhaps a twentieth the size of his sea novels. The rhymes are simple, merry, and meant to be read aloud. It shows the great adventure writer playing gently at the nursery door.
21871-adventures-in-the-far-west:
Young Britons cross the North American West in this short, picture-filled adventure by W. H. G. Kingston. Twenty-nine illustrations crowd the book, including a striking scene of a witch doctor visiting a sick man. The party travels among grizzly bears, wolves, and tribes who do not want them there. For much of the tale they live with a friendly tribe, whose ways Kingston describes at length.

Near the end, the heroes help rescue an emigrant wagon train attacked by a hostile tribe. A young lady has been seized and carried off, and the chase is on. Charley Fielding's cry at the campfire opens the action. Kingston's style, the editor says, is as excellent as ever. It is a brisk western in his classic mold.
22042-christmas-its-origin-and-associati:
William Francis Dawson set out to trace Christmas from its beginnings to his own day. His Christmas: Its Origin and Associations gathers customs scattered through many older authors. He found that some great Christmas feasts marked turning points in English history. He also saw the yearly feast as a link in the chain of Christian evidence across nineteen centuries.

Dawson moves from Roman and pagan roots through medieval revels to Victorian family practice. Holly, mistletoe, carols, feasts, and charity all get their histories. The book is earnest, well stocked, and proud of its subject. It suits readers who want the story behind the holiday's familiar trimmings.
22277-darry-the-life-saver-or-the-heroes:
Frank V. Webster wrote Darry the Life Saver, or The Heroes of the Coast, in 1911 for boy readers. Webster supplied many volumes to the cheap series trade under his own name and others. His hero Darry belongs to the surfmen who guarded America's coasts. The book opens on a brigantine battered by a Caribbean hurricane, staggering along like a wounded beast, her masts gone by the board.

From that wreck the tale builds rescues by breeches buoy and lifeboat. One picture shows a woman lowered safely and stowed away. The Life-Saving Service, forerunner of the Coast Guard, supplies real practice behind the thrills. Darry's adventures honour men who rowed out when others ran from the sea.
2241-love-s-labour-s-lost:
A king of Navarre and three lords swear off women, food, and sleep to study for three years, just as the Princess of France arrives with her ladies. Love's Labour's Lost watches the oath crumble in a festival of puns, songs, and love letters, with the pedant Holofernes and the clown Costard adding to the wordplay. Wit is the real subject here, and everyone competes at it.

Unlike most comedies, the ending defers marriage: the ladies demand a year of proof before they will wed. The play's verbal fireworks and bittersweet close make it a favorite of readers who love language itself. Its songs and jokes reward a slow, attentive reading.
23094-the-boy-nihilist:
Allan Arnold recruits a bright young fellow in The Boy Nihilist. Friends knew his talents well. So did members of the secret societies scattered across Ireland, Germany, and Russia. They knew him as a bright young fellow with brains, pluck, and enthusiasm, which, rightly directed, would make him valuable to any secret organization having the people's liberty at heart.

Beyond that, nothing particular was known of him, which is exactly how dime novels like their conspirators. Plots, bombs, and disguises fill this entry in the era's anxious literature of anarchism. Arnold writes the secret-society scare as boys' adventure. The book survives as a period artifact, showing how 1890s headlines about nihilists were repackaged for young readers hungry for danger.
23155-western-characters-or-types-of-bor:
James Hall apologizes for a gap in Western Characters, his types of border life in the western states. A sketch or two, Hall admits, might have been fuller had certain new books reached him in time. Schoolcraft's large work on Indian history and character heads his list of missed sources.

Hall, an Ohio judge and editor, sketched the frontier's human types while the frontier was still news. Hunters, settlers, preachers, and Native leaders pass through his pages as specimens of a vanishing world. The Schoolcraft aside shows his method, a working writer stitching authorities into firsthand sketches. Published in the 1850s, the book preserves border life described by a man who lived on that border and helped invent its literature.
23179-frictional-electricity-from-the-sa:
Max Adeler's Frictional Electricity is a comic tale that first reached readers through the Saturday Evening Post. An inmate of an asylum begs a visitor to hear him out. He says no nurse will listen to him, though telling his story would do him good after the hard use he has had.

His whole ruin, he claims, came from frictional electricity, a thing his listener admits he does not know. The patient wishes he had stayed just as ignorant, pointing to his own broken state as proof. Adeler frames the piece as a tall, rueful confession, played for laughs and pity at once.
23188-michael-penguyne-or-fisher-life-on:
Michael Penguyne, or Fisher Life on the Cornish Coast tells a story of men and boys who earn their living from the sea. An older fisherman works his sails with one eye on the shore below them. He keeps glancing toward the south-west, where heavy clouds are piling up fast.

Between tasks, he casts a look of approval at the boy with him. That small glance carries the book's world: skill learned by watching, weather read at a glance, and danger judged early. Readers get fisher life as daily work, not as scenery, on a coast where storms build quickly.
23254-the-cobbler-in-the-devil-s-kitchen:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The Cobbler in the Devil's Kitchen comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories. The Kitchen has a natural tiny fireplace on its east side, a couple of feet high. Cedar foliage screens it from the lake wind, and there Owen, the cobbler, cooked his meals.

His hearth had no flue, yet the smoke generally found its way out. Fish then crowded the straits, and Owen had only a short cast to reach deep water. Catherwood sets a solitary tradesman inside a wild, well-stocked place. Readers get a quiet tale of making do, alone, on the lakes.
23287-lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the:
Lavengro, subtitled The Scholar, the Gypsy, the Priest, is a life story told by its own hero. The narrator begins with his father, a Cornish man and the youngest of seven brothers. The family were gentlemen of a modest kind, not very wealthy, yet holders of a coat of arms.

They lived on their own land at Tredinnock. The name means the house on the hill, and the house and its acres had been in their possession from time beyond memory. Readers get an autobiographical tale of learning, wandering, and Romany life, rooted in one old Cornish family's pride and decline.
2503-myths-and-legends-of-california-and:
This collection gathers the myths and legends of California and the Old Southwest, from Native American creation stories to Spanish and Mexican tales of the borderlands. The volume preserves stories of Coyote, of lost mines, and of haunted missions, told in a plain style for general readers. The legends map a region's imagination.

The book's value lies in its range: many peoples' stories side by side. Modern readers should note its early twentieth century framing. Folklore lovers will find a rich regional treasury. The legends include stories from many Native peoples of the region.
26-paradise-lost:
John Milton retells the Fall of Man in blank verse across twelve books. Paradise Lost opens in Hell, where Satan rallies his fallen angels after defeat. The poem then follows creation, temptation, and exile from Eden.

Milton states his aim plainly: to justify the ways of God to men. Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit, lose Paradise, and face a hard world with hope. Satan's pride and rhetoric make him a vivid, troubling figure. The epic stands as the great English poem on sin and grace. Poets and readers have debated Satan's appeal ever since, making the epic a living argument.
2607-psmith-journalist:
P. G. Wodehouse sends his elegant hero Psmith to New York in this comic novel, and opens by warning London readers that New York life runs on different rules. Gangs there, he explains, murder not on impulse but on commercial lines, at so many dollars per murder.

Psmith takes over a newspaper and turns journalist, using wit, nerve, and perfect manners against gangsters and corrupt bosses. Wodehouse writes with his usual lightness, and the jokes never quite hide the danger. The book delights as a farce of a very English gentleman tidying a very American mess.
282-eothen-or-traces-of-travel-brought-h:
A. W. Kingslake crossed from Europe into the Ottoman East and wrote the journey down. Eothen, or Traces of Travel Brought Home from the East, in the 1898 Newnes edition, opens at Semlin on the Danube. Belgrade's fortress looms across the river, dark and historic.

Kingslake notes how two frontier towns, a cannon shot apart, hold no communion. Hungarian, Turk, and Serb live asunder across the Save. Later chapters carry him through Turkey, Syria, and Egypt with wit and observation. The book became a classic of Victorian travel writing. Kingslake's wit and eye for contrast made Eothen a travel classic.
2900-the-age-of-invention-a-chronicle-of:
Holland Thompson wrote The Age of Invention as a chronicle of American inventors, warning that no short book could catalog every nineteenth-century invention. Instead he sketches the personalities behind the machines, leaving technical detail to encyclopedias. The story includes the Waltham mill, where Paul Moody of Amesbury helped build looms, carding, drawing, and roving machines under one roof.

By the autumn of 1814 the Waltham works combined every step of clothmaking in a single American mill, one of the first in the world to do so. Thompson uses such scenes to show invention as teamwork, business, and craft together. The book suits readers who want the human history of American machinery rather than a parts list.
2938-yeast:
Thomas Henry Huxley chose yeast as the subject of a popular lecture for three reasons, simplicity, familiarity, and the chance to explain without diagrams. Yeast is among the simplest and most familiar objects of household life, and its phenomena can be put plainly without turning away to pictures. The lecture follows sugar as it breaks down under fermentation.

Huxley reports that refined analysis accounts for at least ninety-nine percent of the sugar, split into carbonic acid and three other products. He speaks with hesitation before his friend Professor Roscoe, lest he trespass on chemistry's province. The lecture remains a model of popular science, turning a kitchen substance into a lesson about living processes.
3033-the-passing-of-the-frontier-a-chron:
Emerson Hough wrote The Passing of the Frontier, a chronicle of the Old West, published by Yale University Press in 1918. Chapters cover the frontier in history, the range, cattle trails, the cowboy, mines, pathways of the West, Indian wars, cattle kings, and the homesteader. Hough opens by calling the frontier the most stirring, intimate, and beloved word in English, carrying the elan of the French En avant.

The narrative follows gold discoveries in Montana, doubly found by men from California and men heading west, with Francois, called Be-net-see, finding gold on Gold Creek in 1852. News lay dormant until 1857, since the wild country had small ingress or egress. The book gives a romantic yet detailed history of the West's closing, written by a novelist-historian.
3139-the-dove-in-the-eagle-s-nest:
Charlotte M Yonge sets this historical romance in a fierce noble household, where a gentle girl must live among hawks. The Macmillan edition of 1890 reprints a story first issued in two volumes in 1866. W J Hennessy supplied the illustrations. Yonge, a favorite Victorian writer for young readers, builds her tale on contrast: softness against pride, patience against force.

The dove of the title is a girl whose temper refuses the eagle's ways. The nest is a castle world of feud, honor, and hard rule. Readers who enjoy Yonge's moral romances will find her usual strengths here. A firm heroine, a vivid past age, and a plot that tests character under pressure all serve a steady sense of right.
3202-moby-thesaurus-list:
This file holds the Moby Thesaurus, a public domain word list released by its author in January 2001. The documentation notes describe it as the unabridged main thesaurus file, distributed in plain ASCII for the MSDOS systems of its day. Vocabulary files arrive in ordinary text form, so any program can read them without special tools.

A thesaurus of this kind groups words by likeness of meaning, giving writers and software a stock of alternatives for any term. The Moby lists became a standard resource for word games, writing aids, and early language software. Readers opening the file will find data, not prose: long runs of related words, built for lookup rather than for reading straight through.
3203-moby-part-of-speech-list:
This file holds the Moby part-of-speech list, a public domain resource released by its author in January 2001. The documentation describes a part-of-speech file in plain ASCII, distributed for MSDOS systems and meant to be unpacked and read by any program. Its entries tag words with their grammatical roles: noun, verb, adjective, and the rest.

Writers of software use such lists to parse sentences, check grammar, and build language tools. The file gives tags rather than definitions or prose, word after word in plain text. Readers opening it will find a working tool, not a book. It is a plain list from the early age of free language data, still handy wherever a program must know what job a word does.
3204-moby-hyphenation-list:
Where may a long word break at the end of a line? The Moby Hyphenator list, public domain since January 2001, answers that question entry by entry. The documentation describes a hyphenation file in plain ASCII, distributed for MSDOS systems and meant to be unpacked and read by any program. Its business is a single practical question: where may a word be broken at the end of a line?

Typesetters, word processors, and text tools use such lists to divide long words cleanly across lines. The file gives break points rather than definitions or prose, entry after entry in plain text. Readers opening it will find data built for machines and for printers: a working tool from the early age of free language data, still useful wherever text must be laid out well.
3205-moby-pronunciation-list:
Written words become spoken sounds in the Moby pronunciator list, a public domain resource from January 2001 built on the CMU dictionary. The documentation describes a pronunciation file in plain ASCII, built from the CMU dictionary list and distributed for MSDOS systems. Its entries pair written words with their spoken sounds, in a phonetic spelling a program can read.

Speech software, rhyming tools, and reading aids use such lists to turn text into sound. The file gives pronunciations rather than definitions or prose, entry after entry in plain text. Readers opening it will find data for machines: a plain, practical list from the early age of free language data, still useful wherever a tool must say a word aloud.
3323-the-ward-of-king-canute-a-romance-o:
Ottilie A Liljencrantz sets this romance in the Danish conquest of England. The fall of the house of Frode opens it, with Randalin, Frode's daughter, at the center. Where war-dogs kennel, when royal blood is young blood, and before the king follow, leading to the training of Fridtjof the page and the game of swords. Taken captive and the young lord of Ivarsdale carry the tale on.

King Canute himself presides over the story's world: a Danish king ruling an English land, with wards, hostages, and loyalties to settle. Liljencrantz writes the eleventh century as adventure, with courts, camps, and swordplay. Liljencrantz's eleventh century runs on courts, camps, and swordplay, with a page growing toward lordship under a conqueror's eye.
3457-the-man-of-the-forest:
Zane Grey sets this western in the White Mountains, where a lone hunter moves under great fir and spruce trees at sunset. Old Baldy, the highest peak, stands bare and gold in the last light, and the forest seems to swallow the man as he glides through it. He is friendly with an Indian hunter, but he hates the sound of white men's horses in those fastnesses.

The trouble comes from a gang of bad men hidden in the woods, and the novel follows pursuit, ambush, and rescue among the peaks. Grey writes the landscape in rich color and keeps the action moving. Readers who like classic westerns will find his familiar mix: a strong silent hero, a wild country, and a fight between lawless greed and solitary honor.
3547-see-america-first:
Orville Hiestand, working with Charles Herr, offers wayside sketches of American scenery in this outdoor book. The dedication thanks the Herr family, whose love of the great out of doors made the sketches possible. The introduction quotes Emerson on morning light, cloud bars like golden fishes, and nature as medicine for bodies cramped by work.

Hiestand urges readers to see America first, rather than crossing the sea for famous views. His sketches follow hilltops at sunrise, woods, and open horizons, arguing that a day outdoors restores tone to mind and body. The book suits travelers, nature lovers, and readers who enjoy early twentieth century praise for the American landscape.
3660-out-of-the-triangle-a-story-of-the-:
Mary Bamford writes a collection of stories from far places, opening in Alexandria, Egypt. A voice rings through a street, crying that sinners should keep their eyes to the ground, while Heraklas walks by Lake Mareotis, mourning his brother Timokles lost in the desert. Other stories in the book include The Squash of the Esvidos, Comale's Revenge, At the Panaderia, Miss Stratton's Paper, and The Victory of Quang Po.

Bamford writes for young readers, with clear morals and vivid foreign settings, from Egyptian lakes to Chinese villages and Arctic igloos. Her tales mix adventure with lessons in honesty, courage, and kindness. The book suits families who enjoy old fashioned story collections that travel the world in a single volume.
3727-maurice-guest:
Henry Handel Richardson sets this long novel among the music students of Leipzig in the 1890s. Maurice Guest, a young man from abroad, stands before the new Gewandhaus as crowds pour out of a rehearsal, and soon he is caught in a love affair that unmakes him. He adores Louise, a gifted and restless fellow student, who in turn loves the brilliant violinist Schilsky and waits in vain for his letters.

Practice rooms, concerts, boarding houses, and long walks frame a study of obsession, as Maurice watches Louise pine, excuse, and hope against all sense. Richardson writes with close care for mood and music, and the novel grows darker as pride and longing wear the hero down. Readers who like serious fiction about art and passion will find a demanding book that earns its length.
4081-the-alchemist:
Ben Jonson's comedy The Alchemist follows three rogues who run a fake philosopher's stone business from a London house while its master is away. Face, Subtle, and Dol Common promise dupes gold, love, and long life, with chants of hum and buz to sharpen the five senses.

A gull named Dapper must bathe his fingers, wash his eyes, and pay twenty nobles among her grace's servants, dressed in a clean shirt for luck. Jonson's plot spins through greed and gulling at a furious pace. Readers who enjoy sharp, crowded comedy will find a masterpiece of trickery and talk.
4277-two-years-before-the-mast:
Richard Henry Dana wrote this classic of sea life from his own time before the mast. A Harvard student who shipped as a common sailor, Dana sailed from Boston around Cape Horn to California in the 1830s. He worked aloft, handled hides on the coast, and lived under harsh captains and harder weather.

The book made its mark by telling the sailor's life plainly, without romance. Readers learn how a ship was worked, how crews were fed and punished, and what the California hide trade meant in daily labor. It remains a firsthand record of the forecastle, and a text that later reformers quoted for the sailor's cause.
4298-the-paying-guest:
George Gissing built this short novel on a simple domestic idea. Mumford sees an advertisement and suggests taking a paying guest, to keep his wife company during the day. Emmeline, startled, weighs the plan: the rent is heavy, and so is the cost of Clarence's season ticket, but their house at Sutton has room to spare.

The air at Sutton has improved mother and child since they left London, and the guest promises company as well as income. Gissing then shows how a stranger in the house changes a marriage, a household, and its small economies. It is a compact study of suburban life, told with Gissing's dry, watchful humor.
452-lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the-p:
George Borrow tells his own wandering youth in this partly true, partly fancied memoir. Lavengro, scholar and would-be writer, roams England, learns tongues, meets gypsies, and talks with priests, tinkers, and horse dealers. Isopel Berners, a tall gypsy girl, stands out among his roadside friends.

Borrow writes in careless, vivid prose, full of talk, quarrel, and sudden charm. An introduction by Augustine Birrell praises the book's elixir of life and motion. The memoir charms as a picaresque portrait of England on foot, where learning and vagabond freedom share the same road.
4589-all-s-for-the-best:
T. S. Arthur published All's for the Best in 1869, gathering twelve sketches. Their titles run from Faith and Patience and Is He a Christian? through Rich and Rare Were the Gems She Wore, Not as a Child, and Angels in the Heart, to Cast Down but Not Destroyed, Good Ground, and Giving That Doth Not Impoverish. Later pieces ask Was It Murder, or Suicide? They add The Nursery Maid, My Father, and The Christian Gentleman.

The opening sketch meets a doubter who trusted human prudence, walked by his own light, and lost his way, confessing he has no faith in anything. A gentleman answers that he has faith in God, though the doubter shakes his head in bewilderment. Readers get a set of earnest Victorian tales about faith, patience, and conduct. Each is short enough to read alone, and each aims to steady a reader in doubt or sorrow.
4676-outpost:
J. G. Austin, author of Dora Darling, or The Daughter of the Regiment, published Outpost at Boston in 1867. Its contents open with sunshine, the little wife, Cherrytoe, and the children of Merrigoland. They go on to a runaway, Mother Winch, Teddy's little sister, the Fayver, and the night-watch. An empty nest, a trace and a search, Teddy's temptation, and the Cachuco follow.

Later chapters bring Giovanni and Pantalon, a pink-silk dress, beginning a new life, wholesale murder, and Dora Darling herself. A chamber of memories, a letter and an offer, Giovanni's room, and a confession lead to Teddy losing and finding his home. Burroughs' business, man versus dog, a visitor for Mrs. Ginniss, a new patron, and welcome home close the tale. Readers get a long Victorian domestic adventure, full of children, secrets, and second chances.
4701-the-ethics-of-the-dust:
John Ruskin, Slade Professor of Fine Art, wrote The Ethics of the Dust as ten lectures to little housewives on the elements of crystallisation. He dedicates the book, at Christmas 1875, to the real little housewives whose gentle listening and thoughtful questioning enabled him to write it. An old lecturer, of incalculable age, talks with girls named Florrie, Isabel, May, Lily, Kathleen, Lucilla, Violet, Dora, and Egypt.

Lectures run from the valley of diamonds and the pyramid builders, through crystal life, orders, virtues, quarrels, caprice, and sorrows, to home virtues and the crystal rest. Ruskin uses crystals to teach order, patience, and moral conduct, mixing science with fable. Readers get a charming, unusual Ruskin book, where geology becomes a lesson in character, for young readers and for adults who like science told as story.
4702-the-flaming-forest:
James Oliver Curwood opens The Flaming Forest with David Carrigan, sergeant in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, humming softly under a blue northern sky and thanking God he is alive. He blesses McVane, superintendent of N Division at Athabasca Landing, for detailing him to his mission. Glad to travel alone in deep forest, he expects weeks carrying him deeper into his beloved north.

Making noonday tea over a fire at a river's edge, Carrigan concludes for the hundredth time that it is nice to be alone in the world. Green forest crowds like an inundation on three sides of him. His comrades call his task a bad assignment, and danger waits ahead. Readers get a northern police adventure of forest fire, pursuit, and romance, with Curwood's usual snow, rivers, and lonely trails, and a hero who loves the wild he polices.
5301-the-imperialist:
Sara Jeannette Duncan's Imperialist, published in 1904, is set in the Canadian town of Elgin. Old Mother Beggarlegs presides like a venerable stooping hawk over a market stall of gingerbread horses, round cookies, and brown sticky taffy. Children speculate about her past, but she will never tell, and only children have time to wonder.

From that small-town opening, Duncan builds a novel of Canadian politics, imperial loyalty, and the pull of Britain against the United States. The book offers a sharp, witty portrait of a young dominion arguing about its future, through characters rooted in a single Ontario town.
5315-told-in-the-east:
Talbot Mundy's Told in the East, published by Bobbs-Merrill in 1920. It was reprinted in the omnibus Romances of India, and gathers three stories: Hookum Hai, For the Salt Which He Had Eaten, and Machassan Ah. Hookum Hai opens with a blood-red sun resting on a low mud wall, above dried acacia trees, in a landscape of heat and dust.

Mundy writes of India with the colour and pace of popular adventure, following soldiers, traders, and local rulers through loyalty, salt, and honour. Readers get three linked tales of British India, in which oaths and debts matter. Desert roads shape the action, from a writer who knew the region's stories well.
560-mr-standfast:
John Buchan returns Richard Hannay to war work in this sequel to Greenmantle, dedicated to South African troops. Hannay, cured of dyspepsia yet restless, hunts a German spy ring through English villages, Picardy chateaus, and Alpine passes. Andrew Amos, Blenkiron, and a cage of wild birds mark the chase.

Buchan writes with warm, steady vigor, mixing spy craft with Bunyan echoes in chapter titles. The tale ends with an exile's return and a summons for Mr. Standfast himself. The novel stands as a strong wartime adventure, where duty, friendship, and faith carry a man through.
5772-ae-in-the-irish-theosophist:
George William Russell, known as AE, writes on theosophy and mysticism in AE in the Irish Theosophist. Contents include a word on the objects of the Theosophical Society. The Twilight Hour, The Mask of Apollo, and The Secret of Power follow. The Priestess of the Woods, A Tragedy in the Temple, and essays on waking, dreaming, and deep sleep complete the set. Verse by AE closes the collection.

Readers meet Irish mysticism at its most poetic, where myth, vision, and spiritual practice blend. Russell treats consciousness as a landscape to explore, with gods and symbols as guides rather than dogmas. The book suits readers of Yeats's circle, Irish literature, and esoteric thought, offering short, luminous pieces that reward slow, reflective reading.
5952-the-bobbsey-twins-in-the-great-west:
Laura Lee Hope takes the Bobbsey family west for a new round of holiday adventures. Bert and his small brother Freddie appear early, full of plans for snowmen and snowball games, while Flossie and the rest of the household share the trip. The book stands late in a long series of Bobbsey tales.

The western setting gives the children fresh ground to explore and fresh scrapes to get out of. As in the houseboat book, the pleasure lies in family company and small, lively incidents. Young readers follow a familiar set of siblings through unfamiliar country.
6067-the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-rockies-:
Frank Gee Patchin opens with love of a horse, as Tad Butler begs Walter Perkins for two minutes on his pony. Walter hesitates, Tad insists he knows how to ride, and Chunky, whose well-rounded cheeks earned his nickname, backs him up with tales of Texas ponies and a broncho barely saddled once.

The Pony Rider Boys ride the Rockies in search of a lost secret, with Stacy Brown, Ned Rector, and Professor Zepplin along. Patchin writes brisk boy adventure, where riding skill, camp talk, and mountain trails matter most. The boys' pride in the saddle carries them into country that tests it.
6102-from-jest-to-earnest:
E. P. Roe dedicates From Jest to Earnest to his friend of youth and maturer years, Reverend A. Moss Merwin, a missionary in a foreign land who left every earthly ambition open at home. The novel begins with a practical joke and its victim, puzzled and interested, then a little pagan and plain talk.

A sleigh ride and something more, another spell than beauty's, finding one's level, and the other set follow. Midnight vigils, a preacher taught by the pagan, and the dawning light carry Hemstead toward earnestness. Roe turns jest into conversion, showing how a joke can open a life to serious faith.
6384-that-printer-of-udell-s-a-story-of-:
A dying mother prays in broken dialect for Dick, fearing a tough time for him when she is gone. She has had no show and has kept scratching to provide for herself and her boy. Her man is mostly no count and trifling, except when he drinks, and then, she says, God knows how he uses them. Dick, a hollow cheeked wisp of a boy crouching like a frightened animal, creeps to the bed and touches her wasted hand.

Harold Bell Wright's middle western story follows that printer's boy from such a start into print shop life at Udell. A body viewed for identification, a disfigured hand, and a missing little finger raise questions of letters and papers hidden. Dick asks in a whisper whether search was thorough, for people hide important documents. Wright writes uplift through work, faith, and a friend who hoped when others lost hope.
6471-the-children-of-the-new-forest:
Captain Marryat, Royal Navy, sets The Children of the New Forest in 1647, when King Charles the First, defeated after nearly five years of civil war, lay prisoner at Hampton Court. Cavaliers were dispersed, and Cromwell's parliamentary army began to control the Commons. In November, Charles escaped with Sir John Berkely, Ashburnham, and Legg, riding fast toward Hampshire and the New Forest, hoping friends had provided a vessel to France.

No vessel waited, and disappointment followed. A mid passage shows Edward and Humphrey in the forest, laying a body in a grave from a cart before calling their sisters, then debating prayers for the dead. They are not in the Bible, Edward says, so some portion of the Bible must be read instead. Marryat writes a children's story of war, hiding, and family duty in the forest.
6479-lady-mary-and-her-nurse-or-a-peep-i:
Mrs. Traill writes Lady Mary and Her Nurse, subtitled A Peep into the Canadian Forest, as a child's guide to forest life told through a nurse's stories. The flying squirrel opens it, with its food, a story of a wolf, an Indian village, and wild rice. Sleighing, sleigh robes, fur caps, otter skins, an old snow storm, otter hunting, and otter slides follow, with Indian names and remarks on wild animals and their habits.

Lady Mary then reads Mrs. Frazer the history of the squirrel family: grey squirrels on Pine Island, their poor relations the chitmunks, and Velvet Paw at the mill by the rapids. Later chapters add Indian baskets, maple sugar, racoons, Canadian flowers, porcupine, and beaver architecture. A mid passage shows blue jays, blackbirds, field mice, squirrels, and chitmunks busy in wheat fields, filling cheeks with grain. Traill writes Canada for children, creature by creature.
6516-the-suppressed-gospels-and-epistles:
Archbishop Wake gathers writings that early Christian groups held dear, yet later councils set aside from the New Testament as most readers know it. Mary, the infancy tales, Nicodemus, letters of Paul and Clement, Barnabas, Hermas, and the notes of Ignatius all appear here, each with its own chapters. The long title states the case plainly: these books were once prized, then barred after sharp dispute.

Wake adds notes on where each text came from and why its standing was questioned, so a reader can judge the claims for each one. The volume thus serves both as a set of old writings and as a record of how a canon took shape. It suits readers who want to see what the early church read beyond the books that stayed in.
6769-the-people-of-the-mist:
H. Rider Haggard dedicates The People of the Mist, first published in 1894, to his godsons, as a record of primeval and troglodyte imagination and barefaced, flagrant adventure. Chapters bear titles like The Sins of the Father, After Seven Years, The Last Vigil, Otter Gives Counsel, and The Tale of Soa. Leonard swears on the blood of Aca, and a midnight marriage follows.

From a yellow devil's nest to the temple of Jâl, the tale moves through vengeance, disillusion, and a people's strange rites. Haggard writes with the gusto of his African romances. The People of the Mist is a thrilling, old-style lost-world adventure, full of danger and wonder.
6808-woman-on-the-american-frontier-a-va:
William Fowler argues that history, as usually told, records men's deeds in war and statecraft, while women appear only as queens or schemers for power. The story of women's work in great migrations, he says, has been told only in lines where it should fill volumes. His book aims to fill that gap, with heroism, adventures, privations, captivities, and noble lives and deaths of pioneer mothers.

Illustrated with many engravings, the history gathers tales of women on the frontier, from cabins to captivity. Fowler's tone is admiring and earnest. Woman on the American Frontier is a valuable, early tribute to pioneer women, still moving in its rescue of their stories.
6813-lost-in-the-backwoods-a-tale-of-the:
Mrs. Traill's tale of the Canadian forest, first called The Canadian Crusoes, returns in 1882 under a new, more descriptive title, Lost in the Backwoods. Young readers had loved it at first, and the publishers hoped it would please a new generation as well. The opening verse paints a Canadian morning, bright streamers on high, dazzling white snow, and ocean waves on shore.

Children lost in the woods must learn to live by wit, work, and courage, in a romantic adventure of the northern forest. Traill writes with a settler's knowledge and a storyteller's warmth. Lost in the Backwoods is a classic Canadian children's adventure, full of woodcraft and pluck.
6972-lays-from-the-west:
Stella, whose full name appears as M A Nicholl, sings lays from the west in a volume dedicated with gratitude to Missus Spotiswood Ash of Bellaghy in Ireland. A prefatory verse pictures a spirit taking her songs as tiny germs and bidding them root among coming hours and grow into flowers. The opening poem, In the Northwest, sets prairie flowers, blue sky, and sweet air against love of a native land far away.

The poet dreams of broad beech shade in glens beside Lough Neagh, even while poplars quiver and the tall iris blooms by a blue lake. The lays that follow hold that double vision, of a new western home and an old Irish shore. Nicholl writes with simple feeling for exile, landscape, and memory.
6998-the-spanish-chest:
Edna Brown's Spanish Chest opens with a foreword comparing books to a sketch whose painted figures walked out of the picture. Brown says books grow because someone thinks hard about their characters, and her own little book grew that way. It is dedicated to Florence and Clara, who shared a winter in the Channel Islands and have since gone on a longer journey, with verses confessing lines washed in with tears.

An illustration asks what a tiny dotted line across the grounds can mean, as Win inquires into a mystery. Photographs and drawings by John Goss adorn the tale, which mixes nonsense, mocking fears, and feeling. Brown wrote not for critics but for friendly eyes, and the chest at the center holds more than old things.
7074-beauty-and-the-beast:
Marie Le Prince de Beaumont tells Beauty and the Beast as a tale for juvenile readers, ornamented with elegant engravings. A rich merchant with six children, three sons and three daughters, spares no cost for their education and gives them all kinds of masters. His daughters are extremely handsome, above all the youngest, admired from childhood as the little Beauty, a name she keeps as she grows.

Her sisters, proud because they are rich, give themselves ridiculous airs and will visit only persons of quality. The youngest, handsome as she is, proves better than her sisters in temper and heart. A frontispiece shows the Beast attacking the merchant, and the tale that follows turns pride, patience, and love into a household classic.
7107-adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chap:
This closing part of Huckleberry Finn opens at chapter thirty six, once all are reckoned asleep. Huck and Tom slip down the lightning rod, shut themselves in the lean to, and bring out fox fire to work by. They clear four or five feet along the middle of the bottom log, right behind Jim's bed, and plan to dig under it, hidden by Jim's counterpane hanging near the ground.

They dig with case knives till near midnight, hands blistered, with hardly a mark to show for it. Huck jokes this is no thirty seven year job but a thirty eight year job, while Tom sighs and falls to thinking. The closing chapters leave Tom still planning while Huck digs through the night.
722-james-otis-the-pre-revolutionist:
John Clark Ridpath tells the life of James Otis, the Boston lawyer whose speeches against writs of assistance helped spark the American Revolution. Otis argued that taxation without representation broke English liberty. Otis argued against writs of assistance in 1761, a speech John Adams called the start of independence.

Ridpath follows Otis from his early career to his fiery courtroom stand and his later decline, placing him before the better-known patriots. The short life serves as an introduction to a founder whose ideas outlived his mind. Ridpath, a popular historian, wrote the life for general readers, not for scholars alone.
7237-roving-east-and-roving-west:
E. V. Lucas roves east and west in this travel book, opening in India with noiseless feet, the sahib, and the passing show. Birds, towers of silence, and garlands follow, then Delhi, Agra, Lucknow, a tiger, the sacred city, and Calcutta. Japan follows, with its little land, its rope trick, and its quiet scenes, and the contents promise a traveller's eye in both worlds.

Lucas dedicates the book to his host at Raisina and quotes Johnson on the two objects of curiosity, the Christian world and the Mahometan world, with Wordsworth close behind. His sketches favour people, streets, and small encounters over grand sights. The result reads like a notebook kept by a friendly wanderer.
7347-the-lincoln-story-book-a-judicious-:
Henry L. Williams compiled the Lincoln Story Book as a judicious collection of the best stories and anecdotes of the great president, many appearing here for the first time in book form. His preface contrasts two Lincolns. One is the Chicago statue's typical Westerner of forum, rostrum, and tribune at his inauguration under the war-cloud in 1861. The other is the Lincoln dear to common people, the speaker of household words.

That second Lincoln appears long and gaunt, divided between two chairs for comfort, head bent forward, smiling broadly at a tale of his own. Williams gathers the jokes, sayings, and human moments that made that figure beloved. The book preserves Lincoln the storyteller beside Lincoln the statesman.
7352-first-and-last:
H. Belloc's First and Last gathers essays whose contents range from weighing anchor and the reveillon through cheeses, the captain of industry, and the inventor. The views of England, the lunatic, the inheritance of humour, and an old gentleman's opinions on historical evidence complete the first sweep. The absence of the past, St Patrick, lost things, the reading of history, victory, and reality follow. Jose Maria de Heredia, Normandy and the Normans, old things, Hastings, and Roman roads in Picardy join them, with the decline of the book among them.

Belloc's table reads like a mind wandering a library and a landscape at once, sure in opinion and rich in phrase. The reward of letters, eye-openers, the public, entries, companions of travel, and sources of rivers close a miscellany with no dull corner. Readers get Belloc at his most various and dogmatic.
838-jasmin-barber-poet-philanthropist:
Samuel Smiles wrote this life of Jacques Jasmin, the barber-poet of Agen in southern France. Born poor, Jasmin cut hair by day and wrote verse in Gascon by night, winning fame for songs that moved the people. Sainte-Beuve praised him as a poet whose influence might have spared France revolutions.

Smiles follows Jasmin from boyhood in Agen to his triumphs as a singer and giver, for he spent his earnings on the poor. The life is a Smiles lesson in self-help through art and charity. The book gives English readers a vivid portrait of a folk poet, and of the France he sang for.
942-green-mansions-a-romance-of-the-trop:
W. H. Hudson wrote this romance of the tropical forest, about Abel, a Venezuelan traveller who flees into the wild and finds Rima, a mysterious girl of the woods. Rima, who speaks with birds and lives among green mansions of trees, becomes Abel's love and his guide to a world apart from men.

Hudson writes the forest with lush, poetic prose, full of birdsong, mist, and danger. The romance turns tragic, as Abel's world and Rima's cannot both survive. The book, praised by its foreword writer as beyond his power to do justice, remains a beloved classic of nature romance, haunting and beautiful.
945-dust:
Mr. and Mrs. Haldeman-Julius wrote this novel whose chapters trace dust through a life: the dust is stirred, dust in her heart, dust begets dust, dust in his eyes, and Martin battles with dust. Martin's son shakes off the dust, the dust settles, and the dust-bin waits at the end.

The novel uses dust as a figure for the grime of poverty, toil, and small-town life, and for the hope of shaking it off. Its prose is earnest and plain, aimed at readers who know hard work. Dust stands as a period piece of American social fiction, where a family's fate is told through a single, homely image.
a-girl-of-the-limberlost:
Gene Stratton-Porter wrote this novel about Elnora Comstock, a poor Indiana girl who pays for her schooling by collecting moths and butterflies in the Limberlost swamp. The character list at the front describes her plainly: she collects moths to pay for her education and lives the Golden Rule. Her mother, embittered by her husband's death in that swamp, withholds money and love alike.

Across twenty-five chapters Elnora enters high school in hand-me-down shame. With help from the kind Sinton neighbors, she builds her collection into a livelihood. She also sets her heart on a violin and a full education. Philip Ammon, a young visitor, joins the moth hunts and falls in love. The book mixes nature study of the vanishing swamp with a story of endurance at home.
a-lady-of-quality-being-a-most-curious-h:
Frances Hodgson Burnett frames her historical novel as a curious history related by Mr. Isaac Bickerstaff, in the 1896 Frederick Warne edition used here. It begins on November 24, 1690, at Wildairs Hall, where the loud, choleric Sir Jeoffry prepares to hunt. His daughter grows up wild, beautiful, and proud in Queen Anne's England.

Twenty-four chapters follow Mistress Clorinda through horse breaking, suitors, a marriage to an earl, and a deadly war of reputation with a rival beauty. A hidden miniature and a night meeting in a rose garden mark key turns. Burnett mixes costume splendor with a study of a woman too strong for her age's rules.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-:
The final chapters of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, chapters 36 to the last, give Tom Sawyer full command of Jim's escape, and the work proceeds by his book-learned rules. Digging with case-knives quietly swapped for picks, a rope ladder baked in a pie, and warnings written in blood. Jim, patient and chained in his cabin, endures a glory he never asked for.

The escape ends in a night chase, a bullet in Tom's leg, and Jim risking his freedom to nurse the boy. Then the revelation that Miss Watson had already freed Jim in her will. Aunt Polly arrives to untangle the boys' names, Tom pays Jim for his trouble, and Huck, dreading adoption and sivilizing, plans to light out for the Territory ahead of the rest.
ae-in-the-irish-theosophist:
AE in the Irish Theosophist collects the early writings of George William Russell, who signed himself AE, from the journal of Ireland's theosophical circle. Russell opens with a word on the objects of the Theosophical Society, the movement that joined Eastern religion, occult study, and moral renewal. Twenty four prose pieces follow, and a set of thirty nine verses closes the gathering.

Titles map his young mysticism: The Mask of Apollo, The Secret of Power, The Priestess of the Woods, and A Tragedy in the Temple. Essays take up concentration, the element language, and the states of waking, dream, and deep sleep under their Sanskrit names. Tales and meditations turn toward Ireland in The Legends of Ancient Eire and At the Dawn of the Kali Yuga. Russell later became a poet, painter, and agricultural reformer; here his otherworldly Ireland is still being invented, page by page.
all-s-for-the-best:
T. S. Arthur gathered All's for the Best in Philadelphia in 1869, twelve tales of faith under trial. The opening piece, Faith and Patience, argues with a doubter of fifty. Mr. Fanshaw confesses he has no faith in anything at all. His friend Wilkins answers with talk of internal sight, the mind's eye.

Other chapters ask Is He a Christian and weigh cast down, but not destroyed. Giving that doth not impoverish praises open-handed charity. Was It Murder, or Suicide darkens the collection with a mystery. The Nursery Maid, My Father, and The Christian Gentleman close the set. Arthur's Swedenborgian faith, trust in divine order behind appearances, shapes every tale. The title is his doctrine: rightly seen, all works for the best, even sorrow.
an-unsocial-socialist:
George Bernard Shaw begins at a girls' school in an old English country house, where a sensible teacher's quiet evening is broken by a strange arrival. Sidney Trefusis, a rich young widower, has walked out of his marriage and his class to preach socialism. He hides near the school under a false name and stirs every mind he meets.

The schoolgirls, their teachers, and the local gentry all collide with Trefusis's talk about property, marriage, and labor. Shaw fills the novel with debates, letters, and comic scenes at the school and on a model farm. It is fiction used as a platform, written with the wit that later made Shaw famous on the stage.
apess-son-of-the-forest:
William Apess, a Pequot Methodist preacher, published A Son of the Forest in 1829. It is the first published autobiography by a Native American. Apess wrote it himself and issued it at his own cost.

He tells of a poor childhood, beatings by white guardians, service in the War of 1812, and his turn to preaching. Throughout, he protests the theft of Native land and the abuse of Native people. His faith and his anger speak side by side. The book opened a path for Native writers and still stings today. Later editions carried his name as Apess, the spelling used here in the title.
beauty-and-the-beast:
Marie Le Prince de Beaumont's Beauty and the Beast is the classic fairy tale, written for the entertainment of juvenile readers and ornamented with elegant engravings. A very rich merchant has six children, three sons and three daughters, and spares no cost for their education.

The youngest daughter, admired from childhood as the little Beauty, is as good as she is handsome. Her two elder sisters pride themselves on their wealth and keep company only with persons of quality. When fortune turns, Beauty's kindness is tested by the Beast's enchanted castle. Readers of every age will recognise this telling as the source of the tale's most familiar form.
ben-hur-a-tale-of-the-christ:
Lew Wallace built Ben-Hur around Judah Ben-Hur, a Jewish prince of Jerusalem under Roman rule, and his boyhood friend Messala, now a Roman officer. A falling tile injures the Roman governor, and Ben-Hur is condemned to the galleys while his mother and sister vanish into prison. At sea he saves the Roman commander Quintus Arrius, who adopts him and makes him rich.

Freed, Ben-Hur trains Arab horses and beats Messala in the great chariot race at Antioch. His search for his family leads through leper caves to the crowds following Jesus of Nazareth. Wallace frames the revenge story inside the Gospel story, ending at the Crucifixion. The novel became the best-selling American religious epic of its century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Saint-Vaast describes an abbey at Arras, ancient capital of Artois, founded in 667. St. Vaast, born about 453, lived as a recluse, was ordained by St. Remi of Reims, and prepared Clovis for baptism before becoming first Bishop of Arras in 499.

Vaast's labours in planting the faith were blessed by many miracles, and he also took charge of Cambrai for ten years. He died in 540 and was laid in his Arras cathedral. In 667 St. Auburt, the see's seventh bishop, began building a Benedictine abbey on the site of a little chapel Vaast had raised to St. Peter, and Vaast's relics were transferred to the new house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agony-of-chri:
Agony of Christ, from agonia, a struggle, means in profane literature athletes' physical struggle or the mental excitement before conflict. In Scripture it occurs only once, Luke 22:43, for Our Lord's anguish in the Garden of Gethsemani. Remarkably, only Luke mentions the sweat of blood and the angel's visitation.

The authenticity of verses 43-44 narrating these details has been questioned. They are absent not only from the other synoptists but even from Luke in several ancient codices, notably the revised Sinaiticus and codices A and B. Their presence in most manuscripts, uncial and cursive, has sufficed to retain them in critical New Testament editions. Their acceptance by Tischendorf, Hammond, and Scrivener seems to settle authenticity beyond doubt. The sweat of blood is read literally by almost all Catholic exegetes, with medical testimony cited that such haematodrosis, though rare, is neither impossible nor preternatural.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-hoh:
Alexander von Hohenlohe-Waldenburg-Schillingsfürst was a titular Bishop of Sardica, famous for his supposedly miraculous cures, born at Kupferzell in Württemberg in August 1794 and dead at Vöslau in November 1849. He studied at Vienna, Berne, Tyrnau, and Ellwangen, and was ordained a priest in September 1815, serving at Stuttgart and then Munich. After a pilgrimage to Loreto, he became councillor in 1817 and canon of Bamberg in 1821.

About 1821 the cures began. Hohenlohe was healed of a throat pain at Hassfurt through the prayers of a peasant, Martin Michel. In June 1821 he cured the paralytic Princess Mathilda von Schwarzenberg by prayer joined with Michel's. The pope told him to attempt no more public cures, but he continued in private. He named times of prayer for applicants across Europe, England, Ireland, and America, including Ann Mattingly of Washington in 1824. Rome passed no judgment on the supposed miracles, and Catholics were divided.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antichrist:
Antichrist, Greek Antichristos, bears the prefix anti, with varied meanings: antibasileus, an interregnum king; antistrategos, a propraetor; anthoupatos, a proconsul; Homer's antitheos, godlike, elsewhere hostile. By analogy antichristos might mean one resembling Christ; safer to define it by biblical and ecclesiastical usage. Antichrist occurs only in John's Epistles, with parallels in the Apocalypse and Paul's Epistles, fainter ones in the Gospels and Daniel.

St. John supposes early Christians acquainted with teaching on Antichrist's coming. The figure is described more fully in 2 Thessalonians. The day of the Lord will be preceded by revolt and the man of sin's revelation. He will sit in God's temple as God, work lying wonders by Satan's power, and seduce truth's rejecters. But the Lord Jesus shall destroy him with the brightness of His coming. Antichrist will be a human person, perhaps of Jewish extraction, not a demon nor the devil incarnate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archpriest:
An archpriest, or chief of the college of presbyters, aided and represented the bishop in liturgical and religious duties. Much as the archdeacon stood out among deacons as the bishop's special assistant, so the archpriest stood out among priests. Found since the fourth century in many dioceses, the archpriest was as a rule, above all in Rome, where the custom began, the oldest presbyter raised to the rank.
